transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Liu (Hera ML Platform), Sofia Ortiz (Hera Eng), Ibrahim Khan (Hera SRE), Lena Park (Hera Privacy)

Summary (auto): SE walked through a benchmark playbook to get apples-to-apples numbers across hosted/dedicated/on-prem. Talked about prompt set design, load generation artifacts, KV cache behaviour and quantization impacts. Action items: share playbook, schedule on-prem run, produce config matrix.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Um, quick housekeeping, Priya will run the tech portion, I'll chim in on commercial bits at the end. 
[00:18] Marcus: Great, thanks. I'm Marcus, I run ML infra. Our goals are pretty narrow — we need consistent latency under 180ms p50 for conversational prompts, and cost targets that don't blow up. Also, we have a privacy constraint for patient text.
[00:35] Priya: Awesome — that's helpful. To start, I want to align on what "apples-to-apples" means here. For us that is same prompt set, same max tokens, same sequence length distribution, identical batching settings and same warm-start strategy for KV cache. If any of those differ the numbers won't be comparable.
[00:55] Sofia: Quick Q on prompt set — can we reuse your public prompt corpus or do we need to sanitize it for PHI? Lena: we need to ensure PHI is scrubbed out; we cannot send raw patient notes out of network.
[01:12] Priya: Yep, that's a good call. We recommend two parallel prompt sets: a synthetic sanitized real-looking set we provide, and a 1k anonymized in-domain set you provide behind the VPC during the on-prem run. That gives us real-world signal without exfil.
[01:30] Ibrahim: Sounds good. For the on-prem pilot, we'll need to know exactly what node specs you expect — GPUs, memory, if CUDA libs are required. Also any kernel / container hints.
[01:45] Priya: For baseline we usually suggest the same hardware you already run — e.g., A100 40GB or H100 if available. For quantized variants we can run 4-bit and 8-bit profiles which lower vram and often increase throughput, but there are quality tradeoffs. We'll supply container images and a Helm chart to deploy the harness.
[02:05] Alex: Can I flag that part of apples-to-apples is workload shaping — sequence length distributions. If your real traffic is 16–32 tokens but our default tests run 512 sequences, the throughput/latency deltas will be meaningless.
[02:21] Marcus: Our actual traffic is spiky — majority short queries ~30 tokens plus 10% long context probes. We can give a distribution.
[02:33] Priya: Great. Next, load generation. We recommend using k6 for steady-state throughput and a locust or custom client for burst / tail-latency. The harness will simulate reconnections, KV cache misses/hits and can run priming phases.
[02:50] Sofia: How do you model KV cache priming? In prod we have a cache warm-up period but can't afford to pre-prime everything.
[03:02] Priya: We use two-phase runs: a priming phase where we send a representative corpus to fill key-value caches, then a steady-state phase measuring p50/p95/p99. We log cache hit ratios alongside latency so you can correlate. Important: priming should reflect expected user journeys — not every key.
[03:24] Ibrahim: What about continuous batching? We use micro-batching on our side — would that overlap or conflict with Redwood's server batching?
[03:36] Priya: Good question. The runtime has its own smart batching layer. If you batch on the client we can get larger aggregates which helps throughput but increases tail latency. For apples-to-apples we run two modes: client-send-each-request and client-batched where you control inter-request timing. We instrument the batching windows and queue depths.
[03:58] Marcus: And quantization — we need details on quality regressions. Do you run evals automatically?
[04:10] Priya: Yes, we recommend running an eval suite with reference prompt/expected outputs. For the playbook we'll run BLEU/ROUGE and a small human-review set for hallucinations and safety. For clinical PHI we recommend additional privacy-preserving checks. We also provide a delta matrix: latency/cost vs quality for 8-bit and 4-bit variants per model size.
[04:38] Sofia: Network topology — when you say on-prem, do you need inbound peering or outbound only? We have strict egress policies.
[04:47] Alex: For private deployments we can do a fully customer-managed control plane — Redwood provides the runtime images and orchestration, you run the nodes inside your VPC. For the benchmark pilot we often do a VPC peering / private link so we can collect metrics without exposing data. But we can also run a fully air-gapped test if you want.
[05:08] Ibrahim: If we use VPC peering, do you need specific security groups? We'll need a list of ports and supported protocols.
[05:17] Priya: We'll send a checklist — expected: HTTPS 443 outbound to metrics collection endpoint, SSH for debug if permitted (can be disabled), and ephemeral ports for gRPC. Also we'll provide IAM / role hints for KMS usage.
[05:33] Marcus: Can we talk about measurement windows? How long do you run the steady-state to get stable p95 numbers?
[05:41] Priya: We aim for at least 10 minutes steady-state after priming for p50/p95 but for p99 we recommend longer runs — 30–60 minutes, and repeated runs at different times of day. We also do cold-start tests. The harness exports histograms and heatmaps so you can see jitter.
[06:03] Sofia: Regarding apples-to-apples, what about kernel/compiler differences? If we tune CUDA or use custom fused kernels in-house that will change perf.
[06:15] Priya: Right — we capture the full environment: CUDA version, CUDNN, kernel flags, driver versions, and even NUMA placement. Our playbook's config matrix enumerates these and flags any mismatches. For comparisons to third parties, we try to match as closely as possible, but we also report the environment differences in the final spreadsheet.
[06:36] Ibrahim: Ok, what's the recommended batching window for our latency target of 180ms p50?
[06:44] Priya: With 30-token avg requests, we typically see the sweet spot at a 10–15ms batching window for high throughput racks, but that depends on tps. If you need strict 180ms p50, you might constrain batching and lean on hardware parallelism. We'll include recommended batches per target.
[07:02] Marcus: Can you also include cost modeling? We need expected token cost per 1M tokens under different quantization and batching setups.
[07:12] Alex: Yep — we'll produce a per-setup cost estimate (tokenized cost + infra amortized) and call out assumptions. We'll also show sensitivity to sequence length and cache hit ratio — e.g., if KV cache hit rises from 60 to 90% your token cost drops by X% because you avoid full decode.
[07:30] Sofia: About metric collection — how much telemetry is collected? We have privacy constraints.
[07:38] Priya: We collect anonymized token counts, latencies, model version, and cache-hit metrics. No raw prompt text leaves your VPC unless you opt-in. For the on-prem fully air-gapped run, we aggregate locally and exchange only metrics summaries.
[07:56] Lena: That's critical for us. We'll need an attestation of no-PHI leakage.
[08:03] Alex: We'll provide a security checklist and SOC2 artifacts. For the pilot we can sign a limited data processing addendum.
[08:12] Marcus: Great. Now, small deep dive on KV cache behavior — does Redwood store KV per session or per model? How does it handle long-term cache eviction?
[08:24] Priya: KV is per model and per context key. We shard KV across GPUs and have an LRU eviction policy tuned for sequence reuse. For long-run sessions we support sticky routing so a session's KV remains local to a serving shard which improves hit rates. We can also pre-load common prefixes during priming.
[08:48] Ibrahim: Any visibility into cache hits per user? We need to know both aggregated hit ratio and per-session tail misses.
[08:57] Priya: Yes, the harness logs both aggregated hit ratio and session-level histograms. We also flag "cold sessions" where hit ratio is <20% so you can focus tuning.
[09:13] Marcus: On quantization, is there an automated calibration step or do we run manual evals?
[09:20] Priya: We have an automated calibration pipeline that runs representative batches and measures activations to pick scaling parameters, but final QA needs the eval suite and some human checks. We'll provide the calibration tool in the harness.
[09:35] Sofia: About measurement parity — if we run your hosting and our on-prem config we should expect some differences. How should we present the final report to internal stakeholders?
[09:46] Alex: We'll provide a single report with a delta column. Each row is a benchmark scenario (model, quant, batch, seq_len) and columns: p50/p95/p99, throughput, cost, cache_hit, environment notes. We recommend a short executive summary highlighting which configs meet SLAs and which don't.
[10:05] Ibrahim: Any gotchas with Kubernetes node pools? We have mixed GPU types across pools and autoscaler preemption.
[10:14] Priya: Don't mix GPU types in the same node pool for consistent perf. Our runtime expects homogeneous GPU families to avoid cross-GPU binary differences and NUMA issues. For autoscaling, pre-warm images in a daemonset to avoid cold starts. We'll share our Helm-values for nodeSelectors and tolerations.
[10:33] Marcus: Let's talk about experiment reproducibility — random seeds, sampling nondeterminism. How do you ensure two runs are comparable?
[10:42] Priya: We seed RNGs when possible, include model version hash, tokenizer version, and use deterministic decoding when measuring latency-only tests. For quality checks we use stochastic sampling but keep seeds logged so you can reproduce.
[10:58] Sofia: Could we do an initial smoke test on hosted Redwood to verify harness and metrics before on-prem?
[11:05] Alex: Absolutely, we usually run a hosted smoke test to validate scripts and dashboards. Then we run the full on-prem runs. The hosted run also helps calibrate expectations.
[11:15] Marcus: Timeline wise — what's realistic?
[11:18] Priya: Share prompts + infra access this week, we'll send playbook and harness within 2 business days, schedule on-prem test week of Jun 16, run hosted smoke test prior.
[11:27] Ibrahim: I have a question about TLS termination and mTLS for internal traffic. We require mTLS to authenticate clients.
[11:35] Priya: We support mTLS and can integrate with your cert management. We also support customer-managed KMS for model keys.
[11:43] Lena: From privacy side, we'd like an explicit list of telemetry fields collected.
[11:49] Alex: We'll produce a telemetry schema and redacted examples.
[11:54] Sofia: Anything else we should be aware of?
[11:57] Priya: One more nuance — when comparing different vendors, ensure tokenizer versions and tokenization pre-processing match. Tokenization mismatches can cause big differences in token counts and cost.
[12:12] Marcus: Noted. Ok, let's recap.
[12:15] Alex: Recap — Redwood to share benchmark playbook, load harness repo, quant profiles. Priya to make apples-to-apples matrix. Hera to provision VPC peering/air-gap options and sanitized in-domain prompt set. We'll do hosted smoke then on-prem pilot week of Jun 16.
[12:36] Sofia: Sounds good. Who's the owner for each item?
[12:40] Marcus: I'll own provisioning and provide distribution histogram.
[12:44] Ibrahim: I'll handle VPC peering and node prep.
[12:48] Lena: I'll own privacy review and DPA questions.
[12:51] Alex: Great — I'll send the calendar invite for the Jun 16 slot and drop the links. Thanks everyone.
[12:59] Marcus: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
